confidence_note: DB title 'Beden Dili'; book is What Every BODY Is Saying (Navarro with Marvin Karlins). The old TR text's interrogation scene (suspect pulling feet before dangerous questions) could not be verified as in the book and is NOT used. Concepts used (limbic 'honest brain', freeze/flight/fight, feet and legs as telling, turtle effect, pacifying behaviors) are from summaries and Navarro's own framing. Research finds nonverbal cues weak indicators of lying; Navarro stresses baselines and clusters. The brain model is a simplification.
facts: Navarro worked as an FBI counterintelligence agent for about 25 years.
He argues the limbic system reacts to threat automatically and cannot be easily controlled; he calls it the 'honest brain'.
The reactions are freeze, flight and fight.
He claims feet and legs are the most honest part of the body because they are far from conscious attention.
When someone wants to leave, feet may turn toward an exit.
Shoulders rising and the neck shrinking is the 'turtle effect'.
Touching the neck or face to calm down is a 'pacifying behavior'.
Caveat: nonverbal cues are weak lie detectors.
tension: People control their words but not what their feet do.
opening_idea: Open on feet turning toward the door under a table.

lessons.idea: Notice the body's change as a reason to ask, not as a verdict.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A colleague's hand goes to their neck at one question.

reflect_final: When did someone's body tell you something their words did not, and what did you do with that observation afterwards?

use_cases.move: Ask what they think instead of guessing.

use_cases.situation: A partner says 'fine' with a tight jaw.
use_cases.move: Say what you noticed and ask.

use_cases.situation: Noticing your own hand on your neck.

pocket_idea: Feet and shoulders move before words do: treat a body change as a reason to ask, not as proof.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Navarro argues feet are the most honest part of the body because we forget to watch them.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Navarro, ex-FBI, says the limbic system reacts to threat before we think: feet turn to the door, shoulders rise, a hand goes to the neck. Treat it as a reason to ask, not a verdict.
